newsitem.title: IRAQ: Foreign businessmen hungry for Iraqi deals.
newsitem.headline: Foreign businessmen hungry for Iraqi deals.

text.p: Baghdad's smartest hotel, the al- Rasheed, is buzzing with businessmen seeking to make deals to buy Iraqi crude oil and to sell goods to Iraq under an oil-for-food formula with the United Nations.
The businessmen travel around the Iraqi capital in limousines and their destination is usually either the State Organisation for the Marketing of Oil (SOMO) or the trade ministry.
SOMO officials say demand for Iraqi crude is higher than the limited amounts Baghdad will be allowed to export.

"We have one group of clients leaving and another coming," said a SOMO official, refusing to be named. "Our international clientele is back but we are very much restricted by production," said the official.

Iraq's Oil Minister, Amir Muhammad Rasheed, has said oil exports would begin on Tuesday. But in New York, U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa doubted that would be the case, noting that New York-based oil experts or overseers had up to 24 hours to review all contracts.

Under the deal with the U.N. Iraq is permitted exports worth $2 billion in six months on a renewable basis. The proceeds, of which about $1.3 billion will be at Iraq's disposal after deductions for Gulf War repaprations and other U.N. costs, will be primarily used for food and medical supplies to alleviate the suffering of sanctions-hit Iraqis.

Oil Minister Rasheed said last week under current prices Iraq would export a maximum 650,000 barrels per day (bpd). Preference in striking contracts, he said, would be given to companies whose countries took a "favourable stand on Iraq sanctions."
The sale of oil and the purchase of supplies and their distribution has to be conducted under tight U.N. monitoring.
Iraq says it has the capacity to produce up to 2.5 million bpd and its export outlets can handle 2.4 million bpd.
Prior to the imposition of U.N. trade sanctions for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, Iraq exported more than 3 million barrels per day (bpd).

The lifting of the overall curbs on Iraqi oil exports needs clearance from the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) that Baghdad had done all that is required from it under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire resolutions.
European businessmen have so far held two exhibtions in Baghdad since Iraq's November 25 acceptance of U.N. terms for conditions on partial exports.

An all-European trade promotion fair for medical and pharmaceutical products brought together several companies with eyes fixed on the $210 million worth of medical supplies Iraq will be permitted to import under the deal.
The other fair, also all-European, promoted water treatment, supply and distribution products.
